title: Agents, Tools, and Guardrails
summary: Recognize agentic behavior, choose the simplest sufficient design, and place enforceable controls around loops that can affect real systems.
objectives: Distinguish a model response, deterministic workflow, and agentic loop.
Define goals, state, tools, exit conditions, budgets, and human handoffs.
Place enforceable guardrails around permissions, inputs, outputs, actions, and state.
Evaluate and recover from looping, drift, unsafe actions, and incomplete handoffs.

sections.title: Choose the simplest sufficient system
paragraphs: A model call produces an output. A deterministic workflow follows code-defined steps. An agentic loop lets a model choose among tools or actions, observe results, update state, and continue toward a goal. Products such as chat assistants and copilots may contain agentic features, but a product name alone does not prove that every interaction is agentic.

Use an agent only when model-directed adaptation adds value beyond a fixed workflow. Define the user goal, permitted scope, observable completion criteria, unavailable actions, maximum turns, time and cost budgets, and conditions that return control to a person.

code.label: Agent run contract
code.code:
Goal: [BOUNDED OUTCOME]
State: [INPUTS, MEMORY, ARTIFACTS]
Tools: [READ AND ACTION TOOLS]
Authority: [PERMISSIONS AND APPROVALS]
Checks: [STEP AND FINAL POSTCONDITIONS]
Budgets: [TURNS, TIME, COST, CALLS]
Exit: [SUCCESS, STOP, FAILURE, HANDOFF]
Recovery: [RESUME, ROLLBACK, ESCALATE]

sections.title: Run a visible observe, decide, act, and check loop
paragraphs: Each step should expose the current goal, relevant state, selected tool, resolved target, expected effect, and next stopping test. The surrounding application validates tool calls and permissions before execution; the model does not grant itself authority.

Start with one agent and the smallest useful tool set. Add routing, specialist agents, or handoffs only when measured failures show that a simpler design cannot reliably handle the task. Every handoff needs a versioned state contract and a clear owner of the next decision.

sections.title: Evaluate trajectories and final outcomes
paragraphs: A plausible final answer can hide unsafe or wasteful steps. Review the trajectory: tool selection, targets, arguments, state changes, approvals, retries, handoffs, and stop decisions. Verify final postconditions in the affected system.

Build evaluations from representative success, boundary, adversarial, and recovery cases. Measure task completion, policy compliance, tool accuracy, duplicate effects, unnecessary steps, latency, cost, escalation quality, and whether the evidence supports the agent's claimed result.

sections.title: Stop and recover from drift or partial execution
paragraphs: Bounded agents stop on achieved goals, denied authority, invalid state, repeated non-progress, exceeded budgets, unsafe requests, uncertain outcomes, or failed checks. Continuing is not success when the loop has lost a reliable path to the goal.

Persist a resumable checkpoint without secrets, reconcile real side effects, and classify completed, failed, unknown, and unattempted steps. Resume only from verified state. Compensate, roll back, disable a tool, or transfer control when recovery requires different authority.

sections.title: Enforce guardrails outside the model
paragraphs: Use scoped credentials, tool allowlists, typed validation, exact-target approval, data minimization, content and policy checks, rate and cost limits, sandboxing, audit records, postcondition verification, and human handoffs. Treat retrieved content and inter-agent messages as untrusted data.

Layer guardrails because no single prompt, classifier, model, or reviewer covers every failure. Test bypass attempts and fail closed when identity, target, permission, or outcome is uncertain. Guardrails should make safe completion easier while stopping consequences outside the run contract.
sections.callout: The model can recommend a safeguard; the surrounding system must enforce it.

activity.title: Design and challenge a bounded agent loop
instructions: Choose a task that may benefit from adaptation and compare a model call, deterministic workflow, and agentic loop. Justify the simplest sufficient option.
Complete the run contract with goal, state, tools, authority, checks, budgets, exits, handoff, and recovery.
Trace one successful trajectory and record every tool, target, state change, approval, postcondition, and stop decision.
Challenge the design with repeated non-progress, an untrusted tool result, and a timeout after an external write; record the stop and recovery behavior.
evidence: A design comparison and complete run contract tied to an observable goal.
One successful trajectory and three failure trajectories with postcondition, audit, handoff, and recovery evidence.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which part of your task became safer or simpler when you removed autonomy?

cues.text: Distinguish model calls, deterministic workflows, and agentic loops, then choose the simplest sufficient design.
Show goal, state, observe, decide, validate, act, verify, and stop or continue as a bounded loop.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A text loop lists goal and state, observation, decision, deterministic validation, tool action, postcondition check, and stop, continue, or handoff. Reduced-motion mode displays all steps.

cues.text: Demonstrate a visible single-agent trajectory and reject an unmeasured multi-agent expansion.
Ask learners to name one stop condition and one action requiring human approval.
Allow two minutes to define budgets, exits, and handoff.
Evaluate both the trajectory and independently verified final state.
Stop repeated non-progress, reconcile side effects, and resume only from verified state.
Place layered identity, permission, validation, limit, audit, verification, and human controls outside the model.
Check whether the learner can classify a looping assistant and select the enforceable stop response.
Guide the design comparison, run contract, successful trajectory, and three failure challenges.
Begin the check after the learner can classify, bound, verify, stop, and recover an agentic run.

questions.prompt: What most clearly makes an AI workflow agentic?
choices: The model can choose tools or actions and continue in a feedback loop toward a goal
It has a product name containing assistant
questions.explanation: Agentic behavior comes from model-directed workflow execution with tools, state, feedback, and continuation—not branding or model size.

questions.prompt: When is a deterministic workflow preferable to an agent?
choices: When fixed steps can reliably satisfy the goal with less cost and uncertainty
Whenever the task has more than one step
questions.explanation: Use the simplest system that meets the requirement; autonomy adds operational uncertainty and should earn its complexity.

questions.prompt: Where should permission for an irreversible action be enforced?
choices: In the surrounding identity, approval, tool, and authorization system
questions.explanation: Prompts can guide behavior, but external controls must enforce identity, target, permission, and approval.

questions.prompt: An agent repeats similar tool calls without making progress. What is the safest response?
choices: Stop on the non-progress condition, preserve state, reconcile effects, and hand off or recover
Add more tools during the run
questions.explanation: Repeated non-progress is a stop condition; verified state and bounded recovery come before more execution.

questions.prompt: Why should an agent evaluation inspect the trajectory as well as the final answer?
choices: To expose unsafe targets, unnecessary actions, hidden failures, and policy violations behind a plausible result
To avoid checking the real target system
questions.explanation: A final answer can look correct even when the run used unsafe or wasteful actions; trajectory and postcondition evidence reveal that.
